Winnipeg's brick legacy

Many of Winnipeg's brick apartment buildings are decades old, from walk-ups in neighbourhoods like Wolseley, West Broadway and Osborne Village to mid-century buildings across the city. They are often well located and full of character. [CMHC's 2025 report](https://eppd1strscr01.blob.core.windows.net/cmhcprdcontainer/sf/project/archive/housing_markets/rentalmarketreportcanadaandselectedmarkets/rental-market-report-2025-fall-en.pdf) says Winnipeg vacancy rose most in pre-1960 buildings.
But Winnipeg's climate is hard on masonry. When water gets into brick or mortar and freezes, it expands, gradually cracking and breaking down the masonry.
Signs of masonry trouble
Property managers should watch for:
**Spalling:** the face of the brick flaking or breaking off.
**Cracked or missing mortar,** especially at parapets, chimneys and corners.
**Stair-step cracks** following mortar joints, which can indicate movement.
**Bulging or leaning walls.**
**Efflorescence:** white salt deposits showing water moving through the wall.
**Interior water staining** near exterior walls.
**Loose bricks** at parapets, lintels or balconies, which can be a safety hazard.

Some of these are cosmetic. Others point to structural problems that need prompt attention. Bulging or leaning walls and stair-step cracks can point to movement, so get a structural engineer's assessment first.
Our view: deferred masonry gets more expensive every winter

Masonry problems rarely stay small. Every winter, water in a cracked joint freezes, opens the crack further and lets in more water. A small repointing repair today can turn into a rebuild of a wall section within a few winters.
There is also a safety issue. Falling brick from parapets or façades can injure people and expose owners to liability.

blocks.x: On older brick, the mortar matters. [National Research Council guidance](https://nrc-publications.canada.ca/eng/view/ft/?id=cf8bdb19-c68d-4a05-83b2-a7545a2a7422) says repointing mortar should be weaker than the brick or stone and no stronger than the existing mortar, or the masonry can spall.
Loose or leaning parapets, failing lintels, cracked chimneys and any crack that points to movement need a qualified professional's assessment before repairs are scoped.
What affects the cost of repointing?
It depends on the size of the damage, what caused it, access to the wall and how much finishing the repair needs to blend in. In practice, that means:
**How much has failed:** a few joints, or a whole elevation.
**The cause:** gutters, flashing or grading that let water in may need attention too.
**Access:** how the wall can be reached, and what sits below it.
**Matching:** how much brick needs replacing, and how closely mortar and brick can be matched.
**Testing:** older materials may need [asbestos testing](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) before work starts.
**Season:** winter work means enclosing and heating the area, which adds cost.
Our cost guide explains [what moves the price of a renovation](/renovation-cost-winnipeg#cost-drivers). A free written quote after an on-site visit spells out what gets removed and rebuilt.
Paying for it under rent rules

Manitoba's [2027 rent guideline is 3%](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/rentincreaseguideline/currentrentguideline.html), and January 2027 brings more units under regulation, when the [exemption threshold rises to $2,000](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/?archive=&item=75138). That limits how quickly owners can recover large capital costs through normal increases.

The province still lets landlords apply for an [above-guideline increase](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/landlord/aboveguide.html), but on October 30, 2026, Manitoba [cut the share of capital costs that counts by 40%](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/?archive=&item=75837), [to 20%, 15%, 10% or 7.5% of the cost](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/annual/2026/116.php), depending on the item. Only 7.5% of foundation and masonry cost now counts, down from 1/8 (12.5%).
So a masonry job adds 40% less to the allowable increase for the complex than it did before.

A tenant also [owes none of a proposed above-guideline increase](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/) until the Branch issues an order, a change made on October 20, 2026. Claims cover [only costs already paid or billed](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/resource_list/aboveguidelinerentincr.pdf), and [any rebates must be listed](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/resource_list/aguideforlandlords_cover.pdf). Owners planning major masonry work should:
Get a detailed, itemized scope from the contractor.
Keep invoices, permits and photos.
Review the Residential Tenancies Branch requirements before starting.
This is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice. Check your own case with the Residential Tenancies Branch, an accountant or a lawyer.
Building a masonry plan
**Have a qualified person inspect every elevation,** including parapets and chimneys, from a lift or with drone photos where needed.
**Classify issues** as safety, structural or cosmetic.
**Address safety issues immediately,** and keep people clear of anything that could fall.
**Take structural questions to a structural engineer first,** then plan repairs for the next construction season.
**Schedule cosmetic work** with other projects to reduce mobilization costs.
**Re-inspect regularly,** at least every few years.
Masonry work in Winnipeg is seasonal, as mortar needs suitable temperatures to cure. Planning and pricing over the winter allows work to start as soon as weather permits.
What a typical brick repointing project looks like

As a general illustration, a three-storey walk-up with failed mortar on one elevation might start with a detailed inspection, followed by repointing of the affected elevation and replacement of spalled bricks. Work is often completed from scaffolding or a lift during warmer months.
Residents can often stay in place, with some disruption from noise and access restrictions near the work area. Clear communication with tenants helps the project run smoothly.
The bottom line

Winnipeg's older brick buildings are valuable, but they need care. Masonry repair, planned and documented, protects residents, preserves the building and keeps your records ready for an above-guideline application under Manitoba's rent rules.
